column4: God places clearly visible towns at measured stages along the road and tells the travellers to journey through them safely by nights and days; this is a fully provisioned caravan route whose successive markers make the way knowable.
The people ask for longer distances between their journeys and are then scattered; it reverses the measured, visible, safe itinerary of 34:18 into broken travel and dispersion.
The pilgrimage company moves on from Arafat to the Sacred Monument and remembers God there as He guided them after prior error; a named route-marker and divine guidance meet within an actual journey.
As successive communities enter the Fire, each curses the one before it, and the last accuses the first of leading it astray; front and rear of the human procession meet at the wrong destination.
The Flame calls the person who turned his back and withdrew, making the warning fire itself summon the traveller whose bodily direction is away from guidance.
The wrongdoer wishes he had taken a road together with the Messenger, expressing salvation as joining the guide’s course.
The false companion led the speaker away from the Reminder after it arrived; it identifies the rival guide who displaced the Messenger’s road desired in 25:27.
The Messenger asks no payment, only that whoever wills take a road to his Lord; lack of recompense, a chosen way, and the Lord as destination closely meet the section’s giver and Godward course.
The town’s believer tells his people to follow messengers who ask no payment and are themselves rightly guided; rightful leaders, following, guidance, and freedom from recompense coincide.
God answers Satan by identifying a straight path under His authority and then limiting Satan’s power over His servants; the true road is defined against the would-be misleader waiting beside it.
East and west belong to God, and wherever people turn there is God’s face; every physical heading is encompassed by the face the section’s giver seeks.
God guides the human being to the road and leaves a real response between gratitude and ingratitude; showing the route does not erase the traveller’s choice.
God shows the human being the two high roads, a compact image of divinely disclosed alternative routes.
The Quran guides to the course that is most upright, giving the revealed warning the practical work of straightening a route.
The listening jinn describe the post-Mosaic Book as guiding to truth and to a straight road; revelation supplies both correct knowledge and direction.
Moses’ Book is described as a light and guidance for people, directly uniting the fire scene’s two functions in a nonliteral form.
Those who believe in the proof and light of 4:174 and hold fast to God are admitted to mercy and guided to Him on a straight road; the light opens an explicitly Godward path.
The hearers are told not to doubt the Hour and to follow the speaker because this is a straight road; eschatological warning becomes an instruction to fall in behind a guide.
The reminder lets whoever wills take a road to his Lord, stating the warning’s purpose as a freely chosen Godward route.
The same reminder formula again invites whoever wills to take a road to the Lord, a repeated direct formulation of warning as wayfinding.
Satan vows to sit in ambush on God’s straight road, placing the misleader as an obstruction precisely on the route disclosed by guidance.
Moses asks Pharaoh whether he will purify himself and let Moses guide him to his Lord so that he may fear; a human guide offers a Godward road through warning.
God finds the Prophet without the way and guides him; although no literal journey is staged, guidance is remembered as God’s personal recovery of one lacking direction.
God makes steadfast believers leaders who guide by His command, explicitly joining forward communal position to delegated divine guidance.
Abraham’s line is made into leaders guiding by God’s command, another direct formulation of the guide as the community’s divinely authorized front.
Thamud receive guidance but prefer blindness to guidance; the refusal converts a shown road into a chosen inability to see it.
After Moses hurries ahead while his people follow his tracks, God tells him that the Samiri has led them astray; the guide’s separation from the line permits a rival leader to divert it.
Those who turn back after guidance has become clear are enticed by Satan, joining bodily retreat to rejection of a disclosed route.
The community is asked whether it will turn back on its heels if the Messenger dies, exposing the danger that followers reverse course when their leader is no longer visibly ahead.
The condemned find their fathers already astray, identifying the earlier rank of the false procession before 37:70 describes the descendants’ movement behind it.
The descendants hasten along their fathers’ traces, a vivid instance of speed and precedent supplying no guarantee that the trodden road is right.
People insist on following their fathers even when those fathers understood nothing and were not guided; inherited leadership is tested against revelation.
The same ancestral appeal is rejected because the fathers possessed neither knowledge nor guidance, repeating the boundary between a prior track and a true guide.
Whoever blinds himself to the Reminder is assigned a devil as inseparable companion, establishing the false travelling partner whose route appears in 43:37.
The devil companions bar people from the road while their followers suppose themselves guided, showing how a company can move confidently under a false bearing.
At arrival the deluded follower wishes an east-to-west distance from his companion, using the widest directional separation to expose how disastrous that companionship was.
One who opposes the Messenger after guidance is clear and follows a road other than the believers’ is left to that chosen direction and burned in Hell; alternative following reaches the warning fire.
Those who set up rivals lead people away from God’s road and are told that their destination is the Fire, making misdirection and the route’s terminal blaze explicit in one ayah.
A person sets up rivals to mislead from God’s road and is told that his final company is the people of the Fire; false direction determines destination.
Satan calls his party so that they become companions of the Blaze, a rival caller assembling and leading a company toward fire.
The arrogant disputant turns his side to lead others away from God’s road and is promised the punishment of burning, joining bodily orientation, misguidance, and fire.
The people in punishment confess that obedience to their chiefs and great ones led them away from the road; the trusted front rank proves to have been a false guide.
Followed leaders disown their followers when all see punishment and their bonds are cut, revealing the collapse of the company at its destination.
The followers wish for a return so they can disown their leaders, but they will not emerge from the Fire; reversal of course is desired only after the terminal boundary is crossed.
Inside the Fire the weak remind the arrogant that they were their followers and ask for relief, showing the rear of the procession confronting those it followed.
Each company cast into Hell is asked by its keepers whether a warner came to it, directly joining group arrival at fire to the prior warning meant to redirect it.
The arriving company admits that a warner came but was denied, distinguishing absence of guidance from refusal of the warning already given.
The object that calls the back-turner in 70:17 is first identified as the Flame, so the later summons is unmistakably a call issued by fire.
Believers are commanded to protect themselves and their families from a Fire, turning warning into responsibility for steering the whole household away from it.
God brings fire for people from a green tree and they kindle from it, repeating the practical, divinely provided fire-making scene developed more fully in 56:71–73.
God carries His servant by night between two sanctuaries to show him signs; it is a divinely directed nocturnal journey with a known departure and destination.
God makes the earth manageable, commands people to walk its paths and eat His provision, and names resurrection as the final return; road, sustenance, and terminus are held together.
The fire has led Moses to the sacred valley, where he is told to remove his sandals; the distant sign thus discloses the exact place to which he was being directed.
Lot and his household are saved except his wife, who belongs to those who remain behind; the rescue line is defined by one member’s contrary rear position.
Lot’s entire family is saved except an old woman among those left behind, repeating the boundary between the departing company and the one who remains.
Lot and all his family are saved except an old woman among those who stay behind, another compressed recollection of the rearward exception.
The messengers assure Lot that he and his family will be saved except his wife, who is among those remaining behind; the family caravan’s exception is stated before the escape.
God makes night and day successors to one another for whoever wishes to remember or give thanks, supplying an ordered alternation analogous to a continuing procession.
The sun cannot overtake the moon and night cannot outstrip day, each moving in its course; the cosmic sequence clarifies an order in which one member does not displace the next.
On that day the human being is informed of what he sent ahead and what he left behind, transferring front-and-rear language from a caravan’s positions to the temporal reach of deeds.
Every soul learns what it sent ahead and left behind, repeating the moral secondary sense of a divinely known front and rear.
The Hereafter is better and more lasting than the nearer life, adding permanence and value to the section’s paired first and last stages.
Some faces on that day are radiant, preparing the direct Godward gaze stated in 75:23 as the fulfilment of their orientation.
Those radiant faces look toward their Lord, giving the sought Godward direction an eschatological completion.
People are commanded to set their faces at every place of worship and call on God sincerely, giving the face a repeated devotional heading.
People emerge from graves rushing toward a raised goal or marker as if racing to it; the road-marker scene reappears at resurrection with an ominous destination rather than a saving beacon.
The Torah is described as containing guidance and light, another revealed joining of the two functions represented by the section’s fire.
The Gospel is likewise described as containing guidance and light, repeating the formula across a second scripture.
People are commanded to believe in God, His Messenger, and the light He has sent down, identifying revelation as the communal light to be trusted.
At final judgment the earth shines with its Lord’s light as the record is set and judgment begins; the journey’s end is staged under divine illumination rather than night darkness.
